\chapter{The Pronouns, And The Article Hindi Does Not Have}
\label{ch:hi-sarvanam}
\hlchaptermodality{94}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the whole subject-pronoun set including we and they, choose the right oblique pronoun for the person I am addressing, and stop reaching for a word to translate the.}

Read the station sentence a mock paper prints, notice that no word for the appears in it, and ask the liking question at both levels of address.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ham]{\hi{हम} — the word that was already inside hamārā}

\label{lesson:HI-C86-ham}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{hamārā}. You learned it as \textquotedblleft{}our\textquotedblright{} and were told what it was built on. Say that word on its own — you have been carrying it for a chapter without being given it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{हम}}
\textbf{\hi{हम}} (\emph{ham}) — \textquotedblleft{}we.\textquotedblright{}

The possessive chapter said \emph{hamārā} was built on \textbf{\hi{हम}}, and there the matter rested. Here is the word itself.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where Hindi says \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{} and English says \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}}]
\textbf{\hi{हम}} does a second job that has no English equivalent. In much ordinary speech it stands in for \textbf{\hi{मैं}}, \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} when the speaker is being modest or speaking as part of a household:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{said} & \textbf{usually means} \\
\midrule
ham jāte haiṅ & we go — or, often, \emph{I go} \\
hamārā ghar & our house — or \emph{my house} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is the same instinct that made \emph{hamārā parivār} the natural way to say \textquotedblleft{}my family.\textquotedblright{} A Hindi speaker places themselves inside a group by default where an English speaker steps out of it.

A listening paper will play you \emph{ham} where you expect \emph{maiṅ}, and nothing marks the difference but context.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{हम}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ham}, we
  \item the possessive built on it (\emph{hamārā})
  \item \emph{ham} and \emph{maiṅ} one after the other
  \item why a speaker might choose \emph{ham} when talking about themselves
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What possessive is built on \textbf{\hi{हम}}? (\emph{Hamārā}.) What else can \emph{ham} mean besides \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{I}, said modestly or as part of a household.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ve]{\hi{वे} — they, and the respect that looks like a plural}

\label{lesson:HI-C86-ve}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{वह}} and \textbf{\hi{हम}}. You can point at one person and you can include yourself in a group. Say \textquotedblleft{}they,\textquotedblright{} and notice the gap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{वे}}
\textbf{\hi{वे}} (\emph{ve}) — \textquotedblleft{}they.\textquotedblright{}

It is the plural of \textbf{\hi{वह}}, and the relationship is visible: the same word with a different vowel.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the plural that is also a courtesy}]
The same habit you met with \textbf{\hi{आप}} appears here. Hindi shows respect by using a \textbf{plural} form for one person:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{about} \\
\midrule
\hi{वह} & one person, familiar or neutral \\
\textbf{\hi{वे}} & several people — \textbf{or one person spoken of with respect} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{ve ā rahe haiṅ} can be \textquotedblleft{}they are coming\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}he is coming,\textquotedblright{} said of someone senior. This is the third time the pattern has appeared: \emph{āp} for a respected listener, the \textbf{-iye} command for a respected listener, and now \emph{ve} for a respected third person.

In everyday speech many speakers say \textbf{\hi{वो}} for both \emph{vah} and \emph{ve}. Recognise it; write the forms above.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{वे}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ve}, they
  \item \textbf{\hi{वह}} and \textbf{\hi{वे}} together, and hear that only the vowel moves
  \item the two things \emph{ve} can mean
  \item the other place Hindi uses a plural to show respect (\emph{āp})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\hi{वे}} the plural of? (\textbf{\hi{वह}}.) What else can it mean about one person? (Respect.) What do many speakers say for both in conversation? (\emph{Vo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hamẽ / tumhẽ]{\hi{हमें} / \hi{तुम्हें} — what mujhe was all along}

\label{lesson:HI-C86-hamen-tumhen}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{mujhe … pasand hai}. You learned it as a frame for saying what you like. Say the first word on its own and ask what it actually is.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{हमें} and \hi{तुम्हें}}
\textbf{\hi{हमें}} (\emph{hamẽ}) — \textquotedblleft{}to us.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\hi{तुम्हें}} (\emph{tumhẽ}) — \textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} at the \emph{tum} level.

\emph{Mujhe} is the same kind of word: \textbf{\hi{मैं}} in its oblique form, meaning \emph{to me}. The liking frame was never a lump — it was a pronoun in a case, and now the rest of the set arrives with it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same bend, a third time}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{subject} & \textbf{oblique} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\hi{मैं} & \emph{mujhe} & to me \\
\hi{हम} & \textbf{\hi{हमें}} & to us \\
\hi{तुम} & \textbf{\hi{तुम्हें}} & to you \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The possessive chapter bent \textbf{-\hi{आ}} to \textbf{-\hi{ए}} in front of a postposition. The imperative chapter bent the verb to match the listener. Here the pronoun itself bends, and the ending it takes is the nasal \textbf{-\hi{ें}}.

That is three separate systems doing the same thing, which is the reason Hindi rewards a learner who looks for patterns rather than lists: the language keeps asking the same question — \emph{what stands after this word?} — and answering it the same way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{हमें}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\hi{तुम्हें}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{mujhe … pasand hai}, and then the same frame about \emph{us}
  \item what \emph{mujhe} actually is, now that you can see the set
  \item the three subjects and their oblique forms in a run
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{mujhe} the oblique of? (\textbf{\hi{मैं}}.) What ending do these oblique pronouns take? (The nasal \textbf{-\hi{ें}}.) How would you say \textquotedblleft{}we like it\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Hamẽ … pasand hai}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āpko / use]{āpko / use — the paradigm closes}

\label{lesson:HI-C86-aapko-use}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{hamẽ} and \emph{tumhẽ}. Two corners of the set are filled. Say the respectful one and the third-person one, and notice you cannot yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: āpko and use}
\textbf{\hi{आपको}} (\emph{āpko}) — \textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} respectfully. \emph{use} — \textquotedblleft{}to him, to her.\textquotedblright{}

These two are built differently from the last pair. Instead of the nasal ending they take \textbf{\hi{को}} (\emph{ko}), the postposition meaning \emph{to}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{आप}} + \textbf{\hi{को}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{आपको}}
\end{quote}

\emph{Use} is the worn-down version of the same thing: \emph{us} + \emph{ko}, squeezed together by centuries of use, exactly as \emph{maiṅ} + \emph{ko} became \emph{mujhe}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the whole set, at last}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{subject} & \textbf{oblique} \\
\midrule
\hi{मैं} & \emph{mujhe} \\
\hi{हम} & \hi{हमें} \\
\hi{तुम} & \hi{तुम्हें} \\
\hi{आप} & \textbf{\hi{आपको}} \\
\hi{वह} & \emph{use} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five forms, and only the first and the last look irregular — because they are the two that wore down. The middle three still show their parts.

\textbf{\hi{वे}} has one too — \emph{unhẽ} — built the same way, which the review lesson adds.

Note that the level you learned to choose in the possessive and imperative chapters is here too: \emph{tumhẽ} to a friend, \emph{āpko} to a stranger. The same decision, for the fourth time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{आपको}\textquotedblright{}, and name the two pieces it is built from
  \item \emph{use}, and say which subject it belongs to
  \item all five obliques in a run
  \item which one you would use asking a stranger what they like
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What postposition is inside \emph{āpko}? (\textbf{\hi{को}}, \emph{to}.) Which two of the five wore down until their parts stopped showing? (\emph{Mujhe} and \emph{use}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[binā ārṭikal]{binā ārṭikal — the word Hindi does not have}

\label{lesson:HI-C86-koi-article}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{वह}}, \textquotedblleft{}that.\textquotedblright{} Now try to say \textquotedblleft{}the book\textquotedblright{} in Hindi, and read on when you find you have no word for \emph{the}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: there is no article}
\textbf{Hindi has no article.} No word for \emph{the}, and no word for \emph{a}.

This is the largest single structural difference between Hindi and English, and it is worth being told once rather than discovered slowly:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{किताब}} — \emph{kitāb} — can mean \textbf{a book} or \textbf{the book}.
\end{quote}

The bare noun covers both. Nothing is missing from the sentence; the slot the English article fills does not exist.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what does the work instead}]
Hindi has three ways to be more specific when it needs to be, and you have all three already:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{want to say} & \textbf{Hindi reaches for} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
a book, one book & \textbf{\hi{एक}} & ek kitāb \\
that book, the one there & \textbf{\hi{वह}} & vah kitāb \\
plain \textquotedblleft{}book\textquotedblright{} & nothing at all & kitāb \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{एक}} is the numeral \emph{one}, pressed into service when indefiniteness matters — which is why \emph{ek chāy dījiye} is \textquotedblleft{}a tea, please\textquotedblright{} rather than a fixed café formula. It was a number the whole time.

\textbf{\hi{वह}} points, and pointing is how Hindi says \emph{the} when \emph{the} really means \emph{that particular one}.

Most of the time neither is needed, and this is the habit to build: \textbf{do not reach for a word to translate \emph{the}.} There isn't one, and putting \emph{vah} in every place English puts \emph{the} sounds as odd as saying \emph{that book} in English every time you mean \emph{the book}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kitāb}, and give both English meanings it covers
  \item \emph{ek kitāb}, and say what \emph{ek} is doing
  \item \emph{vah kitāb}, and say when you would choose it
  \item what you should do when you want to say \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{} (nothing)
  \item \emph{āpko ek kitāb pasand hai}, and notice there is still no article in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many articles does Hindi have? (None.) What was \emph{ek} before it marked indefiniteness? (The numeral \emph{one}.) What is the commonest correct translation of English \emph{the}? (Nothing at all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sarvanām kī tālikā]{sarvanām kī tālikā — subject and oblique, side by side}

\label{lesson:HI-C86-repaso-sarvanam}



\begin{quote}
Name the five subject pronouns and as many obliques as you can, before reading the table.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the table, complete}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{subject} & \textbf{oblique} \\
\midrule
\hi{मैं} & \emph{mujhe} \\
\hi{हम} & \hi{हमें} \\
\hi{तुम} & \hi{तुम्हें} \\
\hi{आप} & \hi{आपको} \\
\hi{वह} & \emph{use} \\
\hi{वे} & \emph{unhẽ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two of the obliques are visibly \textbf{\hi{को}} attached — \emph{āpko} plainly, \emph{use} after wear. Three take the nasal ending. The set is small and none of it is arbitrary once you know that a postposition is hiding in each one.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the fourth appearance of one decision}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{system} & \textbf{at the tum level} & \textbf{at the āp level} \\
\midrule
possessive & \hi{तुम्हारा} & \hi{आपका} \\
copula & \hi{हो} & \hi{हैं} \\
command & \hi{बोलो} & \hi{बोलिए} \\
\textbf{oblique pronoun} & \textbf{\hi{तुम्हें}} & \textbf{\hi{आपको}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four systems, one decision. Choosing how to address someone settles all four at once, which is why the grid has been worth building across three chapters rather than learning four unrelated lists.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the six subject pronouns
  \item the obliques that take \textbf{\hi{को}}, and the ones that take the nasal
  \item the \emph{tum} row across all four systems
  \item how many articles Hindi has, and what does the work instead
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which postposition is hiding inside every oblique pronoun? (\textbf{\hi{को}}.) How many systems does the level decision now settle? (Four.) What translates English \emph{the}? (Nothing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ham sṭeśan par milẽge]{\hi{हम} \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{पर} \hi{मिलेंगे} — the sentence the paper actually prints}

\label{lesson:HI-C86-sintesis-sarvanam}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{हम}}. Until this chapter the track could not say it, and a reading item that opens with it was unreadable from the first word.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read aloud. Every word has been taught:

\begin{quote}
\hi{हम} \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{पर} \hi{मिलेंगे।} \hi{वे} \hi{भी} \hi{आ} \hi{रहे} \hi{हैं।}
\end{quote}

Two sentences. Note what is \textbf{not} in the first one: no word for \emph{the} in front of \emph{sṭeśan}, because there is none to put there. An English speaker reads \textquotedblleft{}we will meet at \textbf{the} station\textquotedblright{} and supplies the article themselves.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: choosing between the obliques in a real question}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{asking} & \textbf{form} \\
\midrule
a friend & \hi{तुम्हें} \hi{क्या} \hi{पसंद} \hi{है}? \\
a stranger & \hi{आपको} \hi{क्या} \hi{पसंद} \hi{है}? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The frame is the one the track has had since its liking chapter. What is new is that the pronoun in it can now change — it was never a fixed phrase, and the first word was always a pronoun in a case.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{हम} \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{पर} \hi{मिलेंगे}\textquotedblright{}
  \item what an English reader adds that the Hindi does not contain
  \item the liking question to a friend, then to a stranger
  \item one sentence about what you and somebody else will do, using \emph{ham}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What word for \emph{the} appears before \emph{sṭeśan}? (None — Hindi has no article.) Which oblique would you use asking a stranger? (\emph{Āpko}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
